mys_2021_imonst2_03.solutionOverride:
Suppose $e$ edge labels are positive. A face with negative product contains an odd number of positive edges, so the number $f$ of negative faces is at most $2e$, since each edge belongs to two faces. The total number of positive labels is $e+6-f$. If $e\le2$, this is at least $6-e\ge4$; if $e\ge3$, it is at least $3$. Consequently the total sum is at least $3-15=-12$.

To attain this, give positive labels to the top-front edge, bottom-right edge and back-left vertical edge, with all other edges negative. These three edges meet each face exactly once. All six face labels are negative, giving $\boxed{-12}$.

Let the scores in ascending order be $p,p+2,\ldots,p+10$. Their sum is $6p+30\le45$, so $p=0,1$ or $2$.

If $p=0$, the bottom team loses to everyone, including the team with only $2$ points, which is impossible.

If $p=1$, there are six decisive games and nine draws. The bottom team has four losses. The next team, scoring $3$, has either one win and four losses or three draws and two losses. In the first case its four losses are additional to the bottom team's four, a contradiction. In the second case it must draw with the bottom team. The team scoring $5$ therefore beats the bottom team and has one win, two draws and two losses. It must also draw with the $3$-point team. Thus the four bottom-team losses, the two $3$-point-team losses and the two $5$-point-team losses are eight different decisive games, again impossible.

Hence $p=2$. There are three draws, giving six draw appearances. Teams with scores $2,4,8,10$ require at least $2,1,2,1$ draws, respectively (reduce their scores modulo $3$). They account for all six appearances. The fourth team has $6$ points and no draws, so has exactly two wins and three losses.

mys_2021_imonst2_09.reason: The difference-of-squares identity turns the required radical into an explicit rational quotient.

mys_2021_imonst2_09.statementOverride: For rational numbers $x,y$ satisfying $x^5+y^5=2x^2y^2$, prove that $\sqrt{1-xy}$ is rational.

mys_2021_imonst2_10.reason: Vector closure separates rational and irrational components to force equality of opposite sides.
mys_2021_imonst2_10.note: Reviewed against the official complete solution compilation. Original appearance: 2021 IMONST 2, Senior 4.
mys_2021_imonst2_10.solutionOverride:
Its exterior angles are $45^\circ$. Orient the first side horizontally and denote consecutive lengths by $a_0,\ldots,a_7$. The sum of its side vectors is zero. Multiplying the horizontal and vertical equations by $\sqrt2$ gives
$$\sqrt2(a_0-a_4)+(a_1-a_3-a_5+a_7)=0,$$
$$\sqrt2(a_2-a_6)+(a_1+a_3-a_5-a_7)=0.$$
All bracketed quantities are integers. Irrationality of $\sqrt2$ implies $a_0=a_4$, $a_2=a_6$, and both remaining integer expressions vanish. Adding and subtracting those expressions gives $a_1=a_5$ and $a_3=a_7$.

mys_2021_imonst2_11.reason: Recognize nonfriendship as an equivalence relation, then use equal degrees to classify complete multipartite graphs.
mys_2021_imonst2_11.note: Reviewed against the official complete solution compilation. Original appearance: 2021 IMONST 2, Senior 5.
mys_2021_imonst2_11.solutionOverride:
Define two guests to be equivalent if they coincide or are not friends. The stated condition makes this relation transitive; it is also symmetric and reflexive. Thus the guests split into classes, with no friendships inside a class and all possible friendships between different classes.

If there are $n$ guests, every class must have size $n-4$, since each member has exactly four friends outside it. If there are $k$ classes, then $k(n-4)=n$, or
$$(k-1)(n-4)=4.$$
The positive divisor possibilities give $n-4=1,2,4$, hence $\boxed{n=5,6,8}$. They are attained by five singleton classes, three classes of size two, and two classes of size four.

mys_2021_imonst2_12.reason: Build the decimal expansion inductively, choosing an odd leading digit to lift divisibility by a power of five.
mys_2021_imonst2_12.note: Reviewed against the official complete solution compilation. Original appearance: 2021 IMONST 2, Senior 6.
mys_2021_imonst2_12.solutionOverride:
We prove more generally that for every $n\ge1$ there is an $n$-digit multiple of $5^n$ with only odd digits. Start with $5$. Suppose $N=5^nq$ is such a number. Seek the next number as $d10^n+N$, where $d\in\{1,3,5,7,9\}$. Dividing by $5^n$, the divisibility requirement is
$$2^nd+q\equiv0\pmod5.$$
The five permitted digits represent all residues modulo $5$, and $2^n$ is invertible, so exactly one works. Appending it on the left completes the induction.

mys_2022_imonst2_07.reason: Express area using distances to two sides, then use the perimeter condition to identify the incenter.
mys_2022_imonst2_07.note: Reviewed against the official complete solution compilation. Original appearance: 2022 IMONST 2, Junior 4 / Senior 1.
mys_2022_imonst2_07.solutionOverride:
Relabel so the line meets $AB,AC$ at $D,E$. Let the inradius be $r$ and the semiperimeter be $s$. The perimeter condition gives $AD+AE=s$, while the area condition gives $[ADE]=rs/2$.

Let $P=DE\cap AI$, where $AI$ is the internal angle bisector. Its perpendicular distances to $AB,AC$ are equal; call the common distance $x$. Splitting $ADE$ into $ADP$ and $AEP$ gives
$$[ADE]=\frac{x(AD+AE)}2=\frac{xs}2.$$
Hence $x=r$. There is exactly one point on the internal angle-bisector ray at distance $r$ from the sides, namely the incenter. Thus $P=I$.

mys_2022_imonst2_08.reason: Parity gives a necessary multiple-of-four condition; sufficiency requires a carefully signed factor construction in three cases.
mys_2022_imonst2_08.note: Reviewed against the official complete solution compilation. Original appearance: 2022 IMONST 2, Junior 5 / Senior 2.
mys_2022_imonst2_08.solutionOverride:
The answer is all multiples of $4$.

If $n$ is odd, all factors are odd, so their sum is odd. If $n\equiv2\pmod4$, exactly one factor is even and the other $n-1$ factors are odd, again giving an odd sum. Thus $4\mid n$ is necessary.

Write $n=4k$. The following constructions each have sum zero, length $4k$ and product $4k$; every stated number of copies is nonnegative.

* If $k$ is odd, use $2k,-2$, then $2k-2$ copies of $-1$, then $k$ pairs $(1,-1)$.
* If $k\equiv2\pmod4$, use $k,4$, then $k+4$ copies of $-1$, then $(3k-6)/2$ pairs $(1,-1)$.
* If $4\mid k$, use $k,-4$, then $k-4$ copies of $-1$, then $(3k+2)/2$ pairs $(1,-1)$.

For example, the first construction has product $-4k(-1)^{2k-2+k}=4k$; the other two sign counts are even as well. This proves sufficiency.

mys_2022_imonst2_09.reason: A digit-by-digit induction lifts divisibility by 2 while preserving the restricted decimal alphabet.
mys_2022_imonst2_09.note: Reviewed against the official complete solution compilation. Original appearance: 2022 IMONST 2, Junior 6 / Senior 3.
mys_2022_imonst2_09.solutionOverride:
Inductively construct an $n$-digit multiple $N=2^nq$ using only $1,2$. The starting case is $N=2$. Prepend a digit $d\in\{1,2\}$. Then
$$d10^n+N=2^n(d5^n+q).$$
Because $5^n$ is odd, choose $d=1$ if $q$ is odd and $d=2$ if $q$ is even. The parenthesis is even, so the new number is divisible by $2^{n+1}$. Induction reaches $n=2022$.

mys_2022_imonst2_10.reason: Intersecting two diagonals reveals two cyclic quadrilaterals and a short angle chain.
mys_2022_imonst2_10.note: Reviewed against the official complete solution compilation. Original appearance: 2022 IMONST 2, Senior 4.
mys_2022_imonst2_10.solutionOverride:
Put $F=BD\cap CE$. The equality $\angle ADF=\angle AEF$ shows that $A,F,D,E$ are concyclic. Consequently
$$\angle AFE=\angle ADE=\angle ABC,$$
so $A,B,C,F$ are also concyclic (using directed angles if necessary). The two circles now give
$$\angle BAC=\angle BFC=\angle DFE=\angle DAE.$$

mys_2022_imonst2_11.reason: Divide the exponents with remainder, cancel an invertible power modulo the denominator, then exploit a strict size bound.
mys_2022_imonst2_11.note: Reviewed against the official complete solution compilation. Original appearance: 2022 IMONST 2, Senior 5.
mys_2022_imonst2_11.solutionOverride:
Write $r=qs+t$ with $0\le t<s$, and put $M=a^s+b^s$. Since $a$ and $b$ are coprime, $b$ is invertible modulo $M$. Using $a^s\equiv-b^s\pmod M$ in the given divisibility and cancelling $b^{qs}$ gives
$$(-1)^qa^t+b^t\equiv0\pmod M.$$
If $t>0$, both $a^t+b^t$ and $|a^t-b^t|$ are strictly less than $M$. They are nonzero: $a=b$ would contradict $a\ge2$ and coprimality. Thus neither can be a multiple of $M$. Therefore $t=0$, as required.

mys_2022_imonst2_12.reason: Translate the hypothesis to an invertible symmetric matrix over parity; a nontrivial alternating-matrix or subset-bijection argument forces even order.
mys_2022_imonst2_12.note: Reviewed against the official complete solution compilation. Original appearance: 2022 IMONST 2, Senior 6.
mys_2022_imonst2_12.solutionOverride:
Work modulo $2$. Form the $n\times n$ matrix $A$ whose entry $A_{ij}$ is $1$ exactly when teams $i,j$ draw. It is symmetric with zero diagonal. For a set $S$, its indicator vector $v$ satisfies $Av\ne0$ by the hypothesis. Thus $A$ has no nonzero kernel and is invertible.

We show that a symmetric zero-diagonal matrix of odd order cannot be invertible over the two-element field. Expand its determinant as a sum over permutations. Terms with a fixed point vanish. If $n$ is odd, any permutation without fixed points has an odd cycle of length at least three. Select the odd cycle containing the smallest element among all odd cycles, and reverse that cycle. This pairs permutations in a fixed-point-free involution. Symmetry makes the paired products equal, so they cancel modulo $2$. The determinant is zero, a contradiction. Hence $n$ is even.

mys_2023_imonst2_10.reason: A ratio from parallel sides combines with altitude similarity to produce the required cyclic quadrilateral.
mys_2023_imonst2_10.note: Reviewed against the official complete solution compilation. Original appearance: 2023 IMONST 2, Senior 4.
mys_2023_imonst2_10.solutionOverride:
Parallelism and the altitude similarities give
$$\frac{AG}{BF}=\frac{CE}{BF}=\frac{AC}{AB}=\frac{AD}{BD}.$$
Also $\angle GAD=\angle FBD$, both equal to $90^\circ-\angle ACB$. Hence triangles $AGD$ and $BFD$ are similar by two proportional sides and their included angle. It follows that
$$\angle AGD=\angle BFD=180^\circ-\angle AFD,$$
so $A,F,D,G$ are cyclic. Since $\angle GAF=90^\circ$, the opposite angle $\angle GDF$ is also $90^\circ$.

mys_2023_imonst2_11.reason: A triangle-inequality bound must be paired with a near-degenerate construction to prove the constant is sharp.
mys_2023_imonst2_11.note: Reviewed against the official complete solution compilation. Original appearance: 2023 IMONST 2, Senior 5.
mys_2023_imonst2_11.solutionOverride:
The answer is $5$. If $c$ is not the shortest, suppose $b\le c$. The triangle inequality gives $a<b+c\le2c$, so
$$a^2+b^2<4c^2+c^2=5c^2.$$
Thus the implication holds for $m=5$.

For every $m<5$, choose a sufficiently small $\varepsilon>0$ and take
$$a=2-2\varepsilon,\quad b=1-\varepsilon,\quad c=1.$$
These form a triangle, $b<c$, and $a^2+b^2=5(1-\varepsilon)^2>m=mc^2$. Hence no smaller $m$ works.

mys_2024_imonst2_05.reason: Two successive cyclic quadrilaterals convert the unusual 135-degree condition into the target angle.
mys_2024_imonst2_05.note: Reviewed against the official complete solution compilation. Original appearance: 2024 IMONST 2, Primary 5 / Junior 2.
mys_2024_imonst2_05.solutionOverride:
Since $\angle AEC=45^\circ$, the condition $\angle AGC=135^\circ$ makes $A,E,C,G$ cyclic. Thus
$$\angle AGF=\angle AGE=\angle ACE=45^\circ=\angle ADF.$$
Therefore $A,D,G,F$ are cyclic. As the square's diagonals are perpendicular, $\angle AFD=90^\circ$, whence $\angle AGD=90^\circ$. The angles around $G$ now give
$$\angle CGD=360^\circ-135^\circ-90^\circ=135^\circ.$$

mys_2024_imonst2_06.reason: Continuous interpolation of the opposite motions exposes two meeting points whose chord separates all simultaneous positions.
mys_2024_imonst2_06.note: Reviewed against the official complete solution compilation. Original appearance: 2024 IMONST 2, Primary 6 / Junior 3.
mys_2024_imonst2_06.solutionOverride:
Interpolate each jump by continuous motion along its arc at constant speed during that minute. Each frog makes exactly one complete revolution in $n$ minutes, in opposite directions. Their relative angular displacement increases strictly by $4\pi$, so they meet exactly twice in a full period. Neither meeting occurs at an integer time, because red and blue points are distinct.

Call the two meeting points $U,V$. Between these meetings the red frog traverses one of the two arcs from $U$ to $V$, while the blue frog traverses the other. Between the second meeting and the next first meeting the same holds with the complementary arcs. Thus the chord line $UV$ separates their positions except at the two meeting instants. It therefore separates them at every integer time, and the motion repeats after $n$ minutes.

mys_2024_imonst2_08.reason: Compare with triangular numbers, then construct all possible remainders using one or two gaps of size two.

mys_2024_imonst2_08.solutionOverride:
Only $\boxed{2,5}$ fail: one term gives $1$, two terms give $3$ or $4$, and three or more terms give at least $6$.

For $n\ge6$, choose the largest $k$ for which $T_k=k(k+1)/2\le n$, and write $n=T_k+r$ with $0\le r\le k$. If $r=0$, use $1,2,\ldots,k$. If $0<r<k$, raise the final $r$ entries of that list by $1$; exactly one gap becomes $2$. If $r=k$, use
$$1,3,4,\ldots,k,k+2.$$
It has $k$ terms, allowable gaps and sum $T_k+k$. The remaining representable small values are $1,3,4$.

mys_2024_imonst2_09.reason: Interpret each floor sum as counting lattice pairs below the same power-product boundary.

Fixing $v=i$ leaves exactly $\lfloor\sqrt{n/i^3}\rfloor$ choices for $u$, giving the left side. Fixing $u=i$ instead leaves exactly $\lfloor\sqrt[3]{n/i^2}\rfloor$ choices for $v$, giving the right side.

mys_2024_imonst2_10.reason: The residue of 2 to the nth power modulo three gives an explicit formula and a direct recurrence check.

mys_2024_imonst2_11.reason: A modular permutation gives the bijection, while three independent congruence classes explain the cube.
mys_2024_imonst2_11.note: Reviewed against the official complete solution compilation. Original appearance: 2024 IMONST 2, Senior 5.
mys_2024_imonst2_11.solutionOverride:
Multiplication of indices by $2$ modulo $2025$ is a permutation, since $2$ is coprime to $2025$. It maps pairs with index difference $\pm3$ exactly to pairs with difference $\pm6$. Applying it to every chosen index is therefore a bijection between the two families, so $S_1=S_2$.

For the first family, forbidden pairs lie entirely inside a single residue class modulo $3$. The three residue classes are independent and have identical cyclic restriction patterns, each with $675$ positions. If one class has $T$ permissible subsets, then $S_1=T^3$.

mys_2024_imonst2_12.reason: Either a chain of circle and power relations or two circle equations and a radical axis establish the exact collinearity.
mys_2024_imonst2_12.note: Reviewed against the official complete solution compilation. Original appearance: 2024 IMONST 2, Senior 6.
mys_2024_imonst2_12.solutionOverride:
Scale and rotate so that
$$J=(0,0),\ A=(0,1),\ B=(1,1),\ C=(1,0).$$
Then $O=(1/2,1/2)$ and $M=(1/2,1)$. The two circle equations are
$$\omega:\ x^2+y^2-x-y=0,$$
$$\Gamma:\ x^2+y^2+\tfrac12x-\tfrac32y=0.$$
Setting $x=0$ in the second gives $P=(0,3/2)$. Subtracting the equations gives the common chord line $y=3x$, and substituting into $\omega$ yields $Q=(2/5,6/5)$. Also $R=(1,3/4)$. These three points all satisfy $y=3/2-3x/4$, proving the claim.

mys_2025_imonst2_02.reason: The construction starts with 1,2,3 and doubles successive terms so their sum remains a common multiple.

mys_2025_imonst2_08.reason: An exterior-angle comparison uses the cyclic quadrilateral and the bisector.
mys_2025_imonst2_08.note: Reviewed against the official complete solution compilation. Original appearance: 2025 IMONST 2, Pioneer 2. Full statement restored from the reviewed source when the collection was expanded to all difficulties.
mys_2025_imonst2_08.statementOverride: In cyclic quadrilateral $ABCD$, let $E=AB\cap CD$ and $F=AD\cap BC$. The internal bisector of $\angle AED$ meets lines $AD,BC$ at $X,Y$, respectively. Prove that $FX=FY$.

mys_2025_imonst2_09.reason: A useful modulus kills every factorial from the seventh onward, while triangular residues give the obstruction.
mys_2025_imonst2_09.note: Reviewed against the official complete solution compilation. Original appearance: 2025 IMONST 2, Pioneer 3.
mys_2025_imonst2_09.solutionOverride:
For $x\ge7$, the factorial sum is congruent modulo $7$ to
$$1!+2!+\cdots+6!=873\equiv5\pmod7.$$
But the triangular numbers $y(y+1)/2$ have only residues $0,1,3,6$ modulo $7$. Thus $x\le6$.

For $x=1,2,3,4,5,6$ the factorial sums are $1,3,9,33,153,873$. A number $N$ is triangular exactly when $8N+1$ is an odd square. Testing these six values gives only $1,3,153$, with $y=1,2,17$. The answers are $\boxed{(1,1),(2,2),(5,17)}$.

mys_2025_imonst2_10.reason: Simulate multiplication and addition using difference and division, with substantial exceptional-case work because equal operands are forbidden.
mys_2025_imonst2_10.note: Reviewed against the official complete solution compilation. Original appearance: 2025 IMONST 2, Pioneer 4.

mys_2025_imonst2_11.reason: Double-count mixed pairs in columns for the divisibility obstruction, then realize it with four column types.
mys_2025_imonst2_11.note: Reviewed against the official complete solution compilation. Original appearance: 2025 IMONST 2, Pioneer 5.
mys_2025_imonst2_11.solutionOverride:
Count pairs of differently facing coins in the same column. The condition contributes $n/2$ pairs for each of the three choices of rows, so there are $3n/2$ pairs. A column contributes either $0$ pairs if all three coins agree, or $2$ otherwise. Hence $3n/2$ is even, which forces $4\mid n$.

Conversely, if $n=4k$, repeat each of the four column patterns
$$HHH,\quad HHT,\quad HTH,\quad HTT$$
exactly $k$ times. Every pair of rows disagrees in exactly two of these four patterns, so the requirement holds. Thus the answer is precisely the multiples of $4$.

mys_2025_imonst2_12.reason: Translate all three variables by three to obtain a nonnegative expression vanishing only at zero.
mys_2025_imonst2_12.note: Reviewed against the official complete solution compilation. Original appearance: 2025 IMONST 2, Pioneer 6. Full statement restored from the reviewed source when the collection was expanded to all difficulties.
mys_2025_imonst2_12.statementOverride: Find all real triples $(a,b,c)$ with $a,b,c\ge3$ and $ab+bc+ca+9=3a+4b+5c$.

mys_2025_imonst2_13.reason: The gcd identity makes a fixed integer divisible by every positive integer.
mys_2025_imonst2_13.note: Reviewed against the official complete solution compilation. Original appearance: 2025 IMONST 2, Junior 1. Full statement restored from the reviewed source when the collection was expanded to all difficulties.
mys_2025_imonst2_13.statementOverride: Determine all arithmetic progressions $(a_n)_{n\ge1}$ of positive integers for which $\gcd(a_n,a_{2n})=n$ for every positive integer $n$.

mys_2025_imonst2_14.reason: The equal chords from the perpendicular-bisector point lead to an angle chain across two secants and a parallel.
mys_2025_imonst2_14.note: Reviewed against the official complete solution compilation. Original appearance: 2025 IMONST 2, Junior 2.
mys_2025_imonst2_14.solutionOverride:
Use directed angles modulo $180^\circ$, and put $P=DE\cap BC$. Since $DB=DC$, the base angles of $DBC$ agree. The circle through $B,C,D,E,F$ gives
$$\begin{aligned}
\angle EFD&=\angle ECD\\
&=\angle BCD-\angle BCE\\
&=\angle CBD-\angle BCE\\
&=\angle DEC-\angle BCE\\
&=\angle EPB.
\end{aligned}$$
Because $GH\parallel PB$ and $E,P,G,D$ are collinear, this last angle is $\angle EGH$. Thus $\angle EFH=\angle EGH$ modulo $180^\circ$, which is exactly the cyclicity condition.

mys_2025_imonst2_15.reason: Conditioning on all but the first box leaves an unbiased parity switch.
mys_2025_imonst2_15.note: Reviewed against the official complete solution compilation. Original appearance: 2025 IMONST 2, Junior 3. Full statement restored from the reviewed source when the collection was expanded to all difficulties.
mys_2025_imonst2_15.statementOverride: Box $i$ contains one red ball and $i$ blue balls, for $1\le i\le100$. Select one ball uniformly and independently from each box. What is the probability of selecting an odd number of red balls?

mys_2025_imonst2_16.reason: Count at least two forbidden squares on each interior antidiagonal, then match the bound with a boundary path.
mys_2025_imonst2_16.note: Reviewed against the official complete solution compilation. Original appearance: 2025 IMONST 2, Junior 4.
mys_2025_imonst2_16.solutionOverride:
For $n=1$ the answer is $0$. Suppose $n\ge2$. Index squares by $(x,y)$ with $1\le x,y\le n$. The path visits every antidiagonal $x+y=d$, since a step changes $x+y$ by $1$.

Each interior antidiagonal $3\le d\le2n-1$ contains at least two squares without obstacles. For $d\le n+1$, take a visited square on antidiagonal $d-1$; its upper and right neighbors lie in the grid on antidiagonal $d$, and both must be clear. For $d\ge n+1$, take a visited square on antidiagonal $d+1$ and use its lower and left neighbors. The two corner antidiagonals each have one clear square. Hence at least
$$2+2(2n-3)=4n-4$$
squares are clear, leaving at most $(n-2)^2$ obstacles.

For equality, take the path along the bottom row and then the rightmost column. Put obstacles in every square outside the bottom two rows and the rightmost two columns. This gives exactly $\boxed{(n-2)^2}$.

mys_2025_imonst2_17.reason: Two pairs of similar triangles incorporate the external equilateral triangles and sum to a straight angle.
mys_2025_imonst2_17.note: Reviewed against the official complete solution compilation. Original appearance: 2025 IMONST 2, Junior 5.
mys_2025_imonst2_17.solutionOverride:
Cyclicity gives similarities $ABP\sim DCP$ and $ADP\sim BCP$. Adding the equal $60^\circ$ angles supplied by the outward equilateral triangles then yields
$$WAP\sim YDP,\qquad ZAP\sim XBP.$$
For example, $WA/AP=AB/AP=DC/DP=YD/DP$ and $\angle WAP=60^\circ+\angle BAP=60^\circ+\angle CDP=\angle YDP$.

Thus $\angle WPA=\angle DPY$ and $\angle APZ=\angle BPX$. Adding these and using the straight line $BPD$ gives
$$\angle WPZ+\angle YPX
=\angle DPY+\angle YPX+\angle XPB=180^\circ.$$

mys_2025_imonst2_18.reason: Construct a very large half-integer so every relevant binomial expansion has an integer part with enough powers of two.
mys_2025_imonst2_18.note: Reviewed against the official complete solution compilation. Original appearance: 2025 IMONST 2, Junior 6.
mys_2025_imonst2_18.solutionOverride:
No. Take $x=2^{4049}+1/2$. For $1\le k\le2025$, every term except the last in the binomial expansion of $x^k$ is an integer multiple of $2^{2025}$: a term containing $(2^{4049})^i$ with $i\ge1$ has a power of two at least
$$4049i-(k-i)=4050i-k\ge2025.$$
Thus for some integer $N$,
$$x^k=2^{2025}N+2^{-k},\qquad \lfloor x^k\rfloor=2^{2025}N.$$
Their product is $2^{4050}N^2+2^{2025-k}N$, an integer. Yet $x$ is a nonintegral half-integer.

mys_2025_imonst2_19.reason: Optimize a worst-case reachability formula using a strategically chosen residue and AM-GM.
mys_2025_imonst2_19.note: Reviewed against the official complete solution compilation. Original appearance: 2025 IMONST 2, Senior 1.
mys_2025_imonst2_19.solutionOverride:
Choose $k=45$. To reach $a$, move forward to the least multiple of $45$ not smaller than $a$, then backward to $a$. This uses at most $45+44=89$ moves.

For any fixed $k$, put $q=\lfloor2024/k\rfloor$ and consider $a=qk+1\le2025$. Any route to $a$ needs at least $q+1$ forward moves and at least $k-1$ backward moves, hence at least $q+k$ moves. Since $2024=qk+r$ with $r\le k-1$,
$$q+k\ge\frac{2025}{k}+k-1\ge2\sqrt{2025}-1=89.$$
Thus the optimum is $\boxed{89}$.

mys_2025_imonst2_20.reason: The reflected circumcenter of BHC and the orthocenter vector identity reduce chord-midpoint location to a projection.
mys_2025_imonst2_20.note: Reviewed against the official complete solution compilation. Original appearance: 2025 IMONST 2, Senior 2.
mys_2025_imonst2_20.solutionOverride:
Use vector coordinates with $O$ as origin and circumradius $R$. Write the vertex vectors as $a,b,c$. The orthocenter vector is $h=a+b+c$.

The circle through $B,H,C$ has center $o'=b+c=h-a$: its distances to $b,c,h$ are respectively $|c|,|b|,|a|$, all equal to $R$. The midpoint of chord $XY$ is the perpendicular projection of $o'$ onto line $AO$. Because $a\cdot h=0$, this projection is
$$\frac{(h-a)\cdot a}{R^2}a=-a.$$
This is the antipode of $A$ on the original circumcircle, proving the claim.

mys_2025_imonst2_21.reason: Successive differences convert the expression into a symmetric pair-product sum bounded by Cauchy.
mys_2025_imonst2_21.note: Reviewed against the official complete solution compilation. Original appearance: 2025 IMONST 2, Senior 3.
mys_2025_imonst2_21.solutionOverride:
Put $d_1=x_1$ and $d_i=x_i-x_{i-1}$ for $i\ge2$. These are nonnegative and have sum $s=x_n\le n$. The expression becomes
$$\sum_{i<j}d_id_j=\frac12\left(s^2-\sum_{i=1}^nd_i^2\right).$$
By Cauchy's inequality, $\sum d_i^2\ge s^2/n$. Therefore the expression is at most
$$\frac{n-1}{2n}s^2\le\frac{n(n-1)}2.$$
Equality is attained by $d_1=\cdots=d_n=1$, equivalently $x_i=i$. Hence the maximum is $\boxed{n(n-1)/2}$.

mys_2025_imonst2_22.reason: Designing five forced interlocking equal-area polyominoes is substantially beyond the target, and the source construction requires a detailed diagram.
mys_2025_imonst2_22.note: Reviewed against the official complete solution compilation. Original appearance: 2025 IMONST 2, Senior 4. Full statement restored from the reviewed source when the collection was expanded to all difficulties.
mys_2025_imonst2_22.statementOverride: A tile is a finite edge-connected union of unit squares. Do there exist five pairwise distinct, nonrectangular tiles, all of the same area, such that an $m\times n$ rectangle can be tiled using copies of these tiles exactly when both $m$ and $n$ are divisible by $2025$? Rotations are permitted, reflections are forbidden, and a tiling need not use every tile type.

mys_2025_imonst2_23.reason: Reflect the midpoint to create a circle centered at D, then apply a tangent power relation to determine the angle.
mys_2025_imonst2_23.note: Reviewed against the official complete solution compilation. Original appearance: 2025 IMONST 2, Senior 5.
mys_2025_imonst2_23.solutionOverride:
Scale the circumradius to $1$ and choose coordinates $O=(0,0)$, $A=(0,1)$. Then $N=(0,1/2)$ and $D=(d,1)$ because $AD$ is tangent. Since $OM\perp BC$, the right triangle $OMD$ gives
$$DM^2=OD^2-OM^2=d^2+1-OM^2.$$
On the other hand, $DN^2=d^2+1/4$. Their equality forces $OM^2=3/4$.

Thus the distance of chord $BC$ from its circle center is $\sqrt3/2$, so the minor central angle $BOC$ is $60^\circ$. Its inscribed angle at $A$ is either $30^\circ$ or $150^\circ$. The triangle is acute, giving $\boxed{\angle A=30^\circ}$.

mys_2025_imonst2_24.reason: A maximal-set count handles the first bound; the stronger bound requires recursive residue splitting and a concavity estimate.
mys_2025_imonst2_24.note: Reviewed against the official complete solution compilation. Original appearance: 2025 IMONST 2, Senior 6.
mys_2025_imonst2_24.solutionOverride:
For (i), choose a progression-free subset $T$ maximal under inclusion, of size $t$. Every excluded element completes a progression with some pair $a,b\in T$, so it is one of $2a-b,2b-a,(a+b)/2$. Consequently
$$2025\le t+3\binom t2.$$
At $t=36$ the right side is $1926$, and it increases with $t$, so $t\ge37$.

For (ii), set $\alpha=\log_3 2$. We prove by strong induction that every $n$-element integer set has a progression-free subset of size at least $n^\alpha$. The cases $n=0,1$ are immediate. Translate and divide by $3$ repeatedly if all elements have the same residue; these operations preserve progressions, and eventually at least two residue classes are nonempty. Let their sizes, in decreasing order, be $a\ge b\ge c$, with $b>0$.

A three-term progression modulo $3$ has either one residue throughout or all three residues. Therefore progression-free subsets chosen within the two largest classes can be united safely. Induction gives a subset of size at least $a^\alpha+b^\alpha$. Put $t=a/b\ge1$. Concavity of $u^\alpha$ means its increments over intervals of length two decrease, so
$$(t+2)^\alpha-t^\alpha\le3^\alpha-1=1.$$
Hence
$$a^\alpha+b^\alpha\ge(a+2b)^\alpha\ge(a+b+c)^\alpha=n^\alpha.$$
The induction follows. Finally, because $2025<3^7$ and $\alpha-1<0$,
$$2025^\alpha>2025(3^7)^{\alpha-1}=\frac{2025\cdot128}{2187}>118.$$
The integral subset size is therefore at least $119$.

kaz_2024_national_g9_q1.reason: The ratio a/b turns both equations into the same cubic; a monotonicity or factorization argument then identifies it with c.
kaz_2024_national_g9_q1.note: Reviewed all six tasks in each of the 2024 Grade 9, 10 and 11 archive pages; identical tasks merged.
kaz_2024_national_g9_q1.solutionOverride:
Put $t=a/b$. Dividing the first equation by $b^2$ gives $b=t^2-t$, so $t>1$. The second equation now yields
$$c^3-c=a+b=b(t+1)=(t^2-t)(t+1)=t^3-t.$$
Therefore
$$(c-t)(c^2+ct+t^2-1)=0.$$
The second factor is positive because $t>1$ and $c>0$. Hence $c=t=a/b$, proving $a=bc$.

kaz_2024_national_g9_q2.reason: Parity of the board determines whether rotations swap colors; the odd case needs a connected-shape bounding-box argument and sharp obstructing examples.
kaz_2024_national_g9_q2.note: Reviewed all six tasks in each of the 2024 Grade 9, 10 and 11 archive pages; identical tasks merged.
kaz_2024_national_g9_q2.solutionOverride:
If $n$ is even, a quarter-turn swaps the two colors. Every shape of odd size has an unequal color count, so $k=n^2-1$ works. The only larger possibility is the whole board, which has equal counts. Thus the answer is $n^2-1$.

Suppose $n$ is odd. We claim the answer is $2n-3$. A connected shape whose bounding box has width $w$ and height $h$ uses at least $w+h-1$ squares: a spanning tree must contain at least $w-1$ horizontal and $h-1$ vertical edges. A shape with $2n-3$ squares therefore cannot span all rows and all columns. It can be translated one square in some direction, reversing every color. Its size is odd, so this supplies both required imbalances.

For $k=2n-2$, take the entire first row and the next $n-2$ squares down the first column. The two arms together have equal color counts, so every copy is balanced.

For $k\ge2n-1$, start with the entire first row and first column and add squares while maintaining connectedness until size $k$. Its bounding box is the whole board, so no nonzero translation fits. Quarter-turns preserve chessboard colors when $n$ is odd; hence copies cannot have opposite imbalances. This excludes all larger $k$.

kaz_2024_national_g9_q3.reason: A circle centered at the base midpoint encodes an isogonal relation; a disciplined coordinate calculation converts the two parallel lines to a circumcenter-tangent collinearity.
kaz_2024_national_g9_q3.note: Reviewed all six tasks in each of the 2024 Grade 9, 10 and 11 archive pages; identical tasks merged.
kaz_2024_national_g9_q3.solutionOverride:
Choose $M=(0,0)$, $B=(-1,0)$, $C=(1,0)$, $A=(u,v)$ and put $s=u^2+v^2$. The assumptions give $u\ne0$, $v>0$, and $s>1$. The circle centered at $M$ is $x^2+y^2=s$.

Intersecting it with the two side lines gives
$$K=\frac{(-u(s+1)-2s,\ (1-s)v)}{s+2u+1},\qquad
L=\frac{(-u(s+1)+2s,\ (1-s)v)}{s-2u+1}.$$
Solve the two parallel-line equations $X=B+\lambda K=C+\mu L$. Equality of the second coordinates gives $\lambda/(s+2u+1)=\mu/(s-2u+1)$; equality of the first makes their common value $-1/(2s)$. Thus
$$X=\left(\frac{u(s+1)}{2s},\frac{v(s-1)}{2s}\right).$$
The circumcenter and tangent intercept are
$$O=\left(0,\frac{s-1}{2v}\right),\qquad D=\left(\frac{s+1}{2u},0\right).$$
Substitution into the intercept equation of $OD$ gives
$$\frac{X_x}{D_x}+\frac{X_y}{O_y}=\frac{u^2}{s}+\frac{v^2}{s}=1.$$
Therefore $X$ lies on $OD$.

kaz_2024_national_g9_q4.reason: A cyclic weighted sum collapses the three divisibility conditions to a linear sum, which a size bound then rules out.
kaz_2024_national_g9_q4.note: Reviewed all six tasks in each of the 2024 Grade 9, 10 and 11 archive pages; identical tasks merged.
kaz_2024_national_g9_q4.solutionOverride:
Suppose it divides all three, and write $N=a^2+b^2+c^2$. Multiplying the three expressions by $c,a,b$, respectively, and adding gives
$$N\mid abcN+a+b+c,$$
so $N\mid a+b+c$. But $0<a+b+c\le N$, with equality only when $a=b=c=1$. Divisibility forces this equality case. There $N=3$ while each original expression equals $2$, a contradiction.

kaz_2024_national_g9_q5.reason: The two right-angle bisectors fix useful coordinates; identifying the base midpoint as the center requires relating a second circle intersection to those coordinates.
kaz_2024_national_g9_q5.note: Reviewed all six tasks in each of the 2024 Grade 9, 10 and 11 archive pages; identical tasks merged.
kaz_2024_national_g9_q5.solutionOverride:
Take $D=(0,0)$, $A=(0,h)$, $B=(-b,0)$ and $C=(c,0)$. The angle conditions give $h>b,c>0$. Set $u=(h-c)/2$ and $v=(h-b)/2$. Substituting the bisector lines $y=-x$ and $y=x$ into the diameter circles gives
$$P=(-u,u),\qquad Q=(v,v).$$
The base midpoint is $M=(v-u,0)$. Both $MP^2$ and $MQ^2$ equal $u^2+v^2$.

It remains to put $R$ on the circle
$$\Sigma:\ x^2+y^2-2(v-u)x-2uv=0.$$
The circle with diameter $AB$ is $x^2+y^2+bx-hy=0$. On line $AP$, write $(x,y)=(-ut,h-t(h-u))$. Besides $t=0$ at $A$, its intersection with this diameter circle has
$$t=\frac{h(h-u)+bu}{u^2+(h-u)^2}.$$
The difference between the equation of $\Sigma$ and that diameter circle, evaluated at this point, is
$$h^2-2uv-t\bigl(h^2-u(h+c)\bigr)=0,$$
because $h^2-u(h+c)=u^2+(h-u)^2$ and $h^2-2uv=h(h-u)+bu$. Hence $R\in\Sigma$, whose center is $M\in BC$.

kaz_2024_national_g9_q6.reason: Consecutive recurrence equations force all two-step differences to have one sign; positivity rules out descent and a power inequality gives a uniform bound.
kaz_2024_national_g9_q6.note: Also Grade 10 Problem 5 and Grade 11 Problem 5; merged identical appearances. Reviewed all six tasks in each of the 2024 Grade 9, 10 and 11 archive pages; identical tasks merged.
kaz_2024_national_g9_q6.solutionOverride:
Raise the recurrence to the $m$th power and compare adjacent instances:
$$(a_{n+3}+a_{n+2})^m-(a_{n+2}+a_{n+1})^m
=2^m(a_{n+2}^{m-1}-a_n^{m-1}).$$
Since positive powers are strictly increasing, $a_{n+3}-a_{n+1}$ has the same sign as $a_{n+2}-a_n$. Hence all two-step differences have the same sign. They cannot be negative, as that would give an infinite strictly decreasing sequence of positive integers along each parity. Thus $a_{n+2}\ge a_n$.

Put $s_n=a_n+a_{n+1}$. Then $s_{n+1}\ge s_n$, while
$$s_{n+1}^m=2^m(a_n^{m-1}+a_{n+1}^{m-1})<2^m s_n^{m-1}.$$
The strict inequality uses $m-1\ge2$ and positivity. Therefore $s_n^m<2^m s_n^{m-1}$, so $s_n<2^m$. In particular $a_1<s_1<2^m$.

kaz_2024_national_g10_q1.reason: The tangent-chord relation identifies equal angles, and two right triangles supply the proportional sides for a final similarity.
kaz_2024_national_g10_q1.note: Also Grade 11 Problem 1; merged identical appearance. The linked discussion supplies worked geometric solutions. Reviewed all six tasks in each of the 2024 Grade 9, 10 and 11 archive pages; identical tasks merged.

kaz_2024_national_g10_q2.reason: Choose an exponent avoiding zero factors, then freeze every p-adic valuation along a congruence progression while the exponent grows.
kaz_2024_national_g10_q2.note: Also Grade 11 Problem 2; merged identical appearance. Reviewed all six tasks in each of the 2024 Grade 9, 10 and 11 archive pages; identical tasks merged.
kaz_2024_national_g10_q2.solutionOverride:
For fixed $i<j$, the equation $i^{n+j}=j^{n+i}$ is equivalent to $(i/j)^n=j^i/i^j$, and has at most one real solution $n$. There are only finitely many pairs. Hence choose a positive $n_0$ coprime to $d$ for which no factor vanishes.

Let $e$ be the sum of the $p$-adic valuations of the factors at $n_0$, and choose $M$ larger than every individual valuation. For any positive integer $t$, set
$$n=n_0+t\,d(p-1)p^M.$$
Then $\gcd(n,d)=1$. Euler's theorem modulo $p^M$ shows that each factor at $n$ is congruent to its factor at $n_0$ modulo $p^M$, since all bases lie between $1$ and $p-1$. As the original factor's valuation is less than $M$, its valuation is unchanged. Thus the product always has valuation $e$. Choose $t$ large enough that $n>e$. The product is then not divisible by $p^n$.

kaz_2024_national_g10_q3.reason: A lower-bound dichotomy and an iterated multiplicative orbit are needed to force either a constant function or the square function.
kaz_2024_national_g10_q3.note: Also Grade 11 Problem 3; above target difficulty. Reviewed all six tasks in each of the 2024 Grade 9, 10 and 11 archive pages; identical tasks merged. Full statement restored from the reviewed source when the collection was expanded to all difficulties.

sau_2024_f13b64.reason: After finding the natural shifted power, subtract it and compare the highest degree of the error terms to force rigidity.
sau_2024_f13b64.competitionOverride: Saudi Arabia IMO programme — Preselection Test 1
sau_2024_f13b64.note: Exact provenance: Saudi Arabia's IMO 2024 booklet, Selected problems from camps - Preselection tests - Test 1. This is a programme selection/camp paper appearance; original sources of reused questions are not established.
sau_2024_f13b64.solutionOverride:
The leading coefficient $a$ satisfies $a=a^3$, hence $a=\pm1$. Negating a solution gives another solution, so assume $P$ is monic of degree $n\ge1$.

The identity $x^3-7x+6=(x-1)(x-2)(x+3)$ shows that $(x+6)^n$ is a solution. Write
$$P(x)=(x+6)^n+Q(x),\qquad\deg Q<n.$$
If $Q\ne0$ has degree $m$ and leading coefficient $b$, substitute this expression into the equation and cancel the common term $(x^3-7x+6)^n$. The left side has degree $3m$. On the right, the three terms containing one factor $Q$ have total leading term $3b x^{2n+m}$. Terms containing two or three factors $Q$ have strictly smaller degrees, since $m<n$. Hence the right side has degree $2n+m>3m$, impossible.

Thus $Q=0$, and all solutions are $\boxed{P(x)=\pm(x+6)^n\ (n\ge1)}$.

sau_2024_72ce2c.reason: Select prime divisors in one residue class so that two successive Euler-theorem applications can construct a term avoiding all of them.
sau_2024_72ce2c.competitionOverride: Saudi Arabia IMO programme — Preselection Test 1
sau_2024_72ce2c.note: Exact provenance: Saudi Arabia's IMO 2024 booklet, Selected problems from camps - Preselection tests - Test 1. This is a programme selection/camp paper appearance; original sources of reused questions are not established.
sau_2024_72ce2c.solutionOverride:
Every term $a_n$ is odd and congruent to $2$ modulo $3$, so it has a prime divisor congruent to $2$ modulo $3$. Suppose only finitely many such primes ever occur, say $p_1,\ldots,p_k$, and put $M=p_1\cdots p_k$.

Since each $p_i\equiv2\pmod3$, neither $M$ nor $\varphi(M)=\prod_i(p_i-1)$ is divisible by $3$. Choose $n=\varphi(\varphi(M))$. Euler's theorem gives
$$3^n\equiv1\pmod{\varphi(M)},$$
so $\varphi(M)\mid3^n-1$. A second application gives
$$3^{3^n-1}\equiv1\pmod M.$$
Therefore $a_n\equiv3\pmod M$, and none of the $p_i$ divides $a_n$. Yet $a_n$ must have a prime divisor congruent to $2$ modulo $3$, contradicting the list. Thus infinitely many primes divide the sequence.

sau_2024_2a7c3e.reason: Use prime-period binary necklaces to make long forbidden words eliminate only one orbit; a careful orbit count beats the sum of all exclusions.
sau_2024_2a7c3e.competitionOverride: Saudi Arabia IMO programme — Preselection Test 1
sau_2024_2a7c3e.note: Exact provenance: Saudi Arabia's IMO 2024 booklet, Selected problems from camps - Preselection tests - Test 1. This is a programme selection/camp paper appearance; original sources of reused questions are not established.
sau_2024_2a7c3e.solutionOverride:
No. Consider binary words of length $13$, up to cyclic rotation, and repeat each around an infinite periodic sequence. Since $13$ is prime, the two constant words have rotation orbits of size one and all other words have orbit size $13$. There are therefore
$$2+\frac{2^{13}-2}{13}=632$$
periodic sequences up to a shift.

A fixed word of length $\ell\le13$ can occur in at most $2^{13-\ell}$ such sequences: rotate its starting point to the beginning of a period and complete the remaining letters. A word longer than $13$ can occur in at most one sequence, because its first $13$ letters determine the period.

Consequently the chosen words of lengths $5$ through $30$ can eliminate at most
$$\sum_{\ell=5}^{13}2^{13-\ell}+17=511+17=528$$
sequences. At least one sequence avoids every chosen word. Any block of $300$ consecutive letters from it is the required counterexample.

sau_2024_f72f97.reason: A short finite-state recurrence counts binary strings avoiding two different forbidden runs.
sau_2024_f72f97.competitionOverride: Saudi Arabia IMO programme — Preselection Test 2
sau_2024_f72f97.note: Exact provenance: Saudi Arabia's IMO 2024 booklet, Selected problems from camps - Preselection tests - Test 2. This is a programme selection/camp paper appearance; original sources of reused questions are not established.
sau_2024_f72f97.solutionOverride:
Encode delivery by $1$ and no delivery by $0$. We must count length-$19$ strings with neither $11$ nor $000$.

Let $A_n,B_n,C_n$ count valid strings ending respectively in $1$, in a single trailing $0$, and in two trailing zeros. For $n=1$ they are $(1,1,0)$, and appending a symbol gives
$$(A_{n+1},B_{n+1},C_{n+1})=(B_n+C_n,A_n,B_n).$$
In particular $S_n=A_n+B_n+C_n$ satisfies $S_n=S_{n-2}+S_{n-3}$ for $n\ge4$, with $S_1=2,S_2=3,S_3=4$. Iteration gives
$$S_4,\ldots,S_{19}=5,7,9,12,16,21,28,37,49,65,86,114,151,200,265,351.$$
Hence there are $\boxed{351}$ patterns.

sau_2024_1ad8bc.reason: Exploit the ordering through a product of two differences, then apply a weighted Cauchy bound; the upper bound comes from expanding the constraint.
sau_2024_1ad8bc.competitionOverride: Saudi Arabia IMO programme — Preselection Test 2
sau_2024_1ad8bc.note: Exact provenance: Saudi Arabia's IMO 2024 booklet, Selected problems from camps - Preselection tests - Test 2. This is a programme selection/camp paper appearance; original sources of reused questions are not established.
sau_2024_1ad8bc.solutionOverride:
Write $P=x^2+z^2+xy+yz+zx$. Expanding the constraint gives
$$25=(2x+y+2z)^2=4P+y^2+4xz\ge4P.$$
Thus $P\le25/4$, with equality precisely at $(x,y,z)=(5/2,0,0)$.

Because $(y-x)(y-z)\le0$, we have $xy+yz\ge y^2+xz$, and hence
$$P\ge(x+z)^2+y^2\ge\frac{(2(x+z)+y)^2}{5}=5.$$
The second inequality is Cauchy's inequality. Equality requires both $y=x$ or $y=z$ and $x+z=2y$, forcing $x=y=z=1$.

sau_2024_0695e4.reason: Coloring the triangular cells in one half of the hexagon turns the diagonal-crossing count into a fixed color imbalance.
sau_2024_0695e4.competitionOverride: Saudi Arabia EGMO team selection — Test 1
sau_2024_0695e4.note: Exact provenance: Saudi Arabia's IMO 2024 booklet, EGMO Team selection tests - Test 1. This is a programme selection/camp paper appearance; original sources of reused questions are not established.
sau_2024_0695e4.solutionOverride:
Subdivide the regular hexagon into the unit equilateral triangles underlying its rhombus tiling. Color upward-pointing triangles red and downward-pointing triangles blue, rotating the picture so the chosen main diagonal is horizontal. Every diamond consists of one triangle of each color.

Consider the half above the diagonal. It consists of $n$ horizontal strips of triangular cells. In each strip, the lower row of triangle bases is one unit longer than the upper row, so the strip contains one more red than blue triangle. The half-hexagon therefore has exactly $n$ more red triangles.

A diamond entirely inside this half contributes one triangle of each color. A diamond crossing the diagonal is cut into its two constituent triangles, and its upper triangle is always red. Consequently the color excess equals exactly the number of diamonds bisected by the diagonal, which is $n$. Rotating the argument handles each main diagonal.

sau_2024_6778a3.reason: Reduce the three sides to a ratio of symmetric quadratic forms, determine its triangle range, and optimize the resulting one-variable sharp bound.
sau_2024_6778a3.competitionOverride: Saudi Arabia IMO programme — Camp Test 3
sau_2024_6778a3.note: Exact provenance: Saudi Arabia's IMO 2024 booklet, Selected problems from camps - Test 3. This is a programme selection/camp paper appearance; original sources of reused questions are not established.
sau_2024_6778a3.solutionOverride:
Put $S=a^2+b^2+c^2$, $Q=ab+bc+ca$, and $t=\sqrt{Q/S}$. Since $Q\le S$ and the triangle inequalities give
$$2Q-S=a(b+c-a)+b(c+a-b)+c(a+b-c)>0,$$
we have $1/\sqrt2<t\le1$.

For $t=1$ the triangle is equilateral and the proposed inequality is an equality for every $k$. Otherwise rearranging it gives
$$k\le F(t):=\frac{1+2t^2}{2(1+t)}.$$
This function is increasing on $[1/\sqrt2,1]$: its derivative has the sign of $2t^2+4t-1$, which is positive there. Thus $F(t)>F(1/\sqrt2)=2-\sqrt2$, so $k=2-\sqrt2$ works for every triangle.

Taking $a=b=1$ and $c\to0^+$ gives $t\to1/\sqrt2$ and shows that every larger $k$ fails for sufficiently small $c$. Therefore $\boxed{k_{\max}=2-\sqrt2}$.

sau_2024_5429e4.reason: Track the parity of odd entries and use a prime-divisor backward invariant; the two exceptional primes require the no-nontrivial-cube-root lemma.
sau_2024_5429e4.competitionOverride: Saudi Arabia IMO programme — Camp Test 3
sau_2024_5429e4.note: Exact provenance: Saudi Arabia's IMO 2024 booklet, Selected problems from camps - Test 3. This is a programme selection/camp paper appearance; original sources of reused questions are not established.
sau_2024_5429e4.solutionOverride:
Let $N=2023^{2024}$. The replacement
$$F(a,b)=\gcd(2024ab,a^2+254ab+b^2)$$
is odd exactly when $a,b$ have different parity. Thus the parity of the number of odd board entries is unchanged. Since $N\equiv1\pmod4$, initially there are $(N+1)/2$ odd entries, an odd number. The final entry is therefore odd.

For every odd prime $p$, we claim that $p\mid F(a,b)$ implies $p\mid a$ and $p\mid b$. If $p\ne11,23$, this follows from $p\mid ab$ and $p\mid a^2+254ab+b^2$. For $p=11$ or $23$, note $254\equiv1\pmod p$. If $b$ is nonzero modulo $p$, put $t=a/b$; the equation is $t^2+t+1=0$. It gives $t^3=1$, but $p\equiv2\pmod3$, so the only cube root of $1$ is $1$, which does not satisfy the quadratic. Thus $p\mid b$, and then $p\mid a$.

If an odd prime divided the final entry, applying this claim backwards through every merge would make it divide every original entry, including $1$, impossible. The final entry is odd and has no odd prime factor, so it is always $\boxed1$.
sau_2024_5429e4.statementOverride:
The board initially contains all integers $1,2,\ldots,2023^{2024}$. A move erases two entries $a,b$ and writes
$$\gcd(2024ab,a^2+254ab+b^2).$$
After repeated moves only one entry $x$ remains. Determine all possible values of $x$.

sau_2024_f08d2c.reason: Inclusion-exclusion modulo two interacts with a multiplicative residue character, making all integers with two distinct prime factors cancel.
sau_2024_f08d2c.competitionOverride: Saudi Arabia IMO programme — Camp Test 3
sau_2024_f08d2c.note: Exact provenance: Saudi Arabia's IMO 2024 booklet, Selected problems from camps - Test 3. This is a programme selection/camp paper appearance; original sources of reused questions are not established.
sau_2024_f08d2c.solutionOverride:
Negative $n$ and $n=1$ contribute no such $k$, so consider positive odd $n>1$. Define $w(t)=\lfloor t/4\rfloor\pmod2$ for odd positive $t$. Its values modulo $8$ are $0,0,1,1$ at residues $1,3,5,7$, respectively. Checking these four residues shows
$$w(uv)=w(u)+w(v)\pmod2.$$
Let the distinct prime factors of $n$ be $p_1,\ldots,p_r$. Inclusion-exclusion, whose signs all become plus modulo two, gives the desired count's parity as
$$\sum_{J\subseteq\{1,\ldots,r\}}w\!\left(\frac{n}{\prod_{j\in J}p_j}\right).$$
The multiplicative rule rewrites a summand as $w(n)+\sum_{j\in J}w(p_j)$. Summing over all subsets gives
$$2^r w(n)+2^{r-1}\sum_{j=1}^rw(p_j)\pmod2.$$
If $r\ge2$ this vanishes. If $r=1$, it is $w(p_1)$, which is odd exactly when $p_1\equiv5$ or $7\pmod8$. Thus the answers are $\boxed{n=p^a}$, where $a\ge1$ and $p\equiv5,7\pmod8$ is prime.

sau_2024_6972c9.reason: Positivity forces a global quadratic lower bound, which pins down the least parameter; integer inputs and an unbounded shift then prove uniqueness.
sau_2024_6972c9.competitionOverride: Saudi Arabia IMO programme — Camp Test 4
sau_2024_6972c9.note: Exact provenance: Saudi Arabia's IMO 2024 booklet, Selected problems from camps - Test 4. This is a programme selection/camp paper appearance; original sources of reused questions are not established.
sau_2024_6972c9.solutionOverride:
First, $f(y)\ge y^2$ for every $y>0$: otherwise choose $x=y^2-f(y)>0$ in the equation, and cancel $f(y^2)$ to get a sum of positive terms equal to zero.

Put $u=f(1)\ge1$. At $x=y=1$,
$$(1+u)^2\le f(1+u)=2u+m/u,$$
so $m\ge u^3+u\ge2$.

For $m=2$, the function $f(x)=x^2$ works. We prove it is unique. The preceding inequality forces $f(1)=1$. Taking $y=1$ gives
$$f(x+1)=f(x)+\frac{2x^5}{f(x)^2}+1,$$
and induction yields $f(n)=n^2$ for all positive integers $n$.

Now put $y=n$ in the original equation and use the lower bound at $x+n^2$:
$$f(x)+\frac{2x^5n^2}{f(x)^2}+n^4\ge(x+n^2)^2.$$
Equivalently,
$$f(x)-x^2\ge2xn^2\left(1-\frac{x^4}{f(x)^2}\right).$$
If $f(x)>x^2$, the right side tends to infinity as $n\to\infty$, a contradiction. Thus $f(x)=x^2$ everywhere. The least parameter is $\boxed{m=2}$.

sau_2024_f4a1ee.reason: Use reflection symmetry of the ordered reduced residues to force an alternating residue pattern, then construct coprime numbers near n/2 that violate it.
sau_2024_f4a1ee.competitionOverride: Saudi Arabia IMO programme — Camp Test 4
sau_2024_f4a1ee.note: Exact provenance: Saudi Arabia's IMO 2024 booklet, Selected problems from camps - Test 4. This is a programme selection/camp paper appearance; original sources of reused questions are not established.
sau_2024_f4a1ee.solutionOverride:
The answers are $\boxed{2,4,10}$, whose reduced-residue lists are $(1)$, $(1,3)$ and $(1,3,7,9)$.

Assume $n$ has the stated property. If $n\ge3$ is odd, its first two reduced residues are $1,2$, impossible. Thus $n$ is even. If $3\mid n$, the two reduced residues straddling $n/2$ sum to $n$, again impossible.

Now $3\nmid n$. Reflection $a\mapsto n-a$ reverses the reduced-residue list. If consecutive residues have sum $s$, the reflected pair has sum $2n-s$. Neither can be zero modulo $3$, so necessarily $s\equiv n\pmod3$. Starting at $a_1=1$, all reduced residues must therefore alternate between $1$ and $n-1$ modulo $3$.

If $n\equiv2\pmod3$ and $n>2$, the reduced residue $3$ contradicts this pattern, which in this case permits only residue $1$. Thus $n\equiv1\pmod3$, and the pattern permits only residues $0,1$.

If $n=12k+4$ with $k\ge1$, the positive integer $n/2-3=6k-1$ is coprime to $n$: a common divisor would divide $6$, while $6k-1$ is odd and not divisible by $3$. But it is $2$ modulo $3$, contradiction. If $n=12k+10$ with $k\ge1$, use instead $n/2-6=6k-1$; its gcd with $n$ divides $12$ and is again $1$. The only remaining cases are $n=4,10$, together with $2$.

idn_2021_national_q2.reason: Two circle-power identities combine with the median formula; the possible relative positions of the second intersections also need checking.
idn_2021_national_q2.note: National. Reviewed all 8 national tasks in each of 2021 and 2022 and all 12 provincial tasks (8 short answer, 4 proof) in the 2024 booklet. Primary author solution archive; not represented as an official organizing-body publication.
idn_2021_national_q2.solutionOverride:
Write $AD=DB=c$, $AE=EC=b$, $BC=2a$, $CD=t$ and $DM=DN=s$. Since $D$ lies inside the circumcircle of $ABC$, $M$ lies on the ray from $D$ opposite $C$. Power at $D$ gives $st=c^2$.

Power of $C$ with respect to the circle $ADE$ gives $CD\cdot CN=CA\cdot CE=2b^2$. If $N$ were on the same side of $D$ as $M$, then $CN=t+s$, so $t^2+c^2=2b^2$. But the median formula gives $t^2=2a^2+2b^2-c^2$, forcing $a=0$, impossible. Thus $N$ is on the other side. It cannot lie beyond $C$, since $C$ has positive power, so $CN=t-s$. Hence $t^2-c^2=2b^2$. Comparing with the median formula now gives $a=c$, or $BC=AB$.

idn_2021_national_q3.reason: The even terms recur every three positions; their 2-adic valuations restrict where the only possible small even term can occur.
idn_2021_national_q3.note: National. Reviewed all 8 national tasks in each of 2021 and 2022 and all 12 provincial tasks (8 short answer, 4 proof) in the 2024 booklet. Primary author solution archive; not represented as an official organizing-body publication.
idn_2021_national_q3.solutionOverride:
The answer is $7$, attained by $5,2,7,9,16,25,41$.

Suppose there are eight terms. If $a_1,a_2$ are both even, they are powers of $2$. Their sum is a power of $2$ only when they are equal, but then $a_4=3a_1$ is not a prime power. Otherwise the parity pattern has one even term every three positions. If an even term $a_i=2^u$ has the following three terms available, then
$$a_{i+3}=a_i+2a_{i+1}.$$
Here $a_{i+1}$ is odd. If $u\ge2$, the right side is divisible by $2$ but not by $4$ and exceeds $2$, so it cannot be a prime power. Therefore such an $a_i$ must equal $2$.

The first even term has index $1$, $2$ or $3$. At index $3$ it is the sum of two odd prime powers, hence at least $6$, already impossible since $a_6$ exists. At index $1$ or $2$ it must be $2$, but the next even term, at index $4$ or $5$, is greater than $2$ and still has three following terms. This is again impossible.

idn_2021_national_q4.reason: An inner square-root estimate uses the fixed sum, followed by a cyclic pairing of outer square roots; the orientation of the cycle is the main insight.
idn_2021_national_q4.note: National. Reviewed all 8 national tasks in each of 2021 and 2022 and all 12 provincial tasks (8 short answer, 4 proof) in the 2024 booklet. Primary author solution archive; not represented as an official organizing-body publication.
idn_2021_national_q4.solutionOverride:
Since $2\sqrt y\le y+1$,
$$2\sqrt{x+\sqrt y}\le\sqrt{4x+2y+2}=\sqrt{8+2x-2z}.$$
Thus it is enough to compare the cyclic sums of the latter square roots. The inequality $\sqrt u+\sqrt v\le2\sqrt{(u+v)/2}$ gives
$$\sqrt{8+2x-2z}+\sqrt{8+2z-2y}\le2\sqrt{8+x-y}.$$
Add this inequality and its two cyclic counterparts, then divide by $2$. All radicands are positive because $x,y,z$ lie between $0$ and $3$.

idn_2021_national_q6.reason: First manufacture the gcd of the whole collection, then use it as a permanent tool to decrease every other entry to that value.
idn_2021_national_q6.note: National. Reviewed all 8 national tasks in each of 2021 and 2022 and all 12 provincial tasks (8 short answer, 4 proof) in the 2024 booklet. Primary author solution archive; not represented as an official organizing-body publication.
idn_2021_national_q6.solutionOverride:
If all entries are already equal, stop. Otherwise retain one entry as an accumulator. Pair it successively with each other original entry whose value differs from the accumulator, keeping the gcd as the new accumulator. An equal entry can be skipped. No performed move creates zero, since its two values differ. After this process the accumulator is the gcd $g$ of all the initial entries.

Every current entry is a positive multiple of $g$. Whenever an entry is $kg$ with $k>1$, pair it with the accumulator $g$. The new values are $g$ and $(k-1)g$. Thus the accumulator survives and the other entry decreases by $g$. Repeating finitely many times makes every entry equal to $g$.

idn_2021_national_q8.solutionOverride:
Exactly $9999/3=3333$ tiles are used, so $H+V=3333$.

Color columns by their indices modulo $3$. The three color classes have sizes $3400,3300,3300$. A horizontal tile covers one square of each color, and a vertical tile covers three of one color. Modulo $3$, the uncovered square must belong to the class of size $3400$ and $H\equiv0\pmod3$. Comparing that class with either smaller class gives $3(V_1-V_2)=99$, so $V\ge33$. Coloring rows the same way gives $V\equiv0\pmod3$ and $H\ge33$.

Conversely leave the upper-left square empty. Tile the remaining $99$ squares of its row horizontally, using $33$ tiles, and the remaining $99$ squares of its column vertically, using $33$ tiles. The remaining $99\times99$ square splits into $1089$ blocks of size $3\times3$. Each block may use three horizontal or three vertical tiles independently. Thus precisely
$$H=33+3r,\qquad V=33+3(1089-r),\qquad 0\le r\le1089,$$
are possible.

idn_2022_national_q1.solutionOverride:
Setting $x=y$ shows that $0$ belongs to the image. Choose $t$ with $f(t)=0$, and put $a=f(0)$. The equation at $(t,t)$ gives $f(a)=0$. At $(0,a)$, its left side is $f(f(a)+f(a))=a$, while its right side is $-a$. Hence $a=0$.

Taking $x=0$ now gives $f(f(y))=f(y)$. Taking $y=0$ gives $f(f(f(x)))=-f(x)$. But the first identity makes this same left side equal to $f(x)$. Therefore $f(x)=0$ everywhere, and this function indeed works.

$$k=ef(b^2+c^2),\qquad l=(1-e)(1-f)(b^2+c^2).$$
The powers of $A$ with respect to the two circles give $AG\cdot AB=AI\cdot AD=k$, with directed lengths if necessary. The powers of $C$ similarly give $CH\cdot CB=CJ\cdot CD=l$. Hence
$$G=(k/b,0),\ I=(0,k/c),\ H=(b,c-l/c),\ J=(b-l/b,c).$$
Let $T=\frac{k}{k+l}(b,c)$. Direct subtraction gives
$$T-G=\frac{k}{k+l}(J-G),\qquad T-I=\frac{k}{k+l}(H-I).$$
Thus $T$ lies on $GJ$, $IH$ and $AC$.

idn_2022_national_q4.reason: A parity reduction leaves five points modulo 13; counting pair midpoints forces two additive collisions whose overlap creates an isosceles triangle.
idn_2022_national_q4.note: National. Reviewed all 8 national tasks in each of 2021 and 2022 and all 12 provincial tasks (8 short answer, 4 proof) in the 2024 booklet. Primary author solution archive; not represented as an official organizing-body publication.
idn_2022_national_q4.solutionOverride:
At least five selected vertices have indices of the same parity. They lie on a regular $13$-gon, whose vertices we label by $\mathbb Z/13\mathbb Z$. It suffices to show that any five-element set $S$ contains distinct $u,v,w$ with $u+w=2v$: those three vertices form an isosceles triangle with apex $v$.

Suppose no such triple exists. Each of the ten unordered pairs in $S$ has its midpoint outside $S$, leaving eight possible midpoint residues. A midpoint can occur for at most two pairs, since pairs with the same midpoint are disjoint and $S$ has only five elements. Therefore at least two distinct midpoints each occur twice.

Each such collision uses four elements. The two four-element sets cannot be identical: two different pairings of the same four elements with equal sums force two elements to coincide, since $2$ is invertible modulo $13$. Relabel so the first collision is $a+b=c+d$ and the second uses $a,b,c,e$. It cannot be $a+b=c+e$, as then $d=e$. If it is $a+c=b+e$, the two equations give $2a=d+e$; if it is $b+c=a+e$, they give $2c=d+e$. Either is the forbidden triple. This proves the claim.

idn_2022_national_q7.reason: Classifying the connected components requires a lexicographic extremal argument, two local reversal improvements, and recognition of the isolated alternating words.
idn_2022_national_q7.note: National. Reviewed all 8 national tasks in each of 2021 and 2022 and all 12 provincial tasks (8 short answer, 4 proof) in the 2024 booklet. Primary author solution archive; not represented as an official organizing-body publication.
idn_2022_national_q7.solutionOverride:
The answer is $2025$. The number of ones is invariant. In addition, the two fully alternating words are isolated: an even-length block has equal counts and cannot be reversed, while an odd-length alternating block reads the same backwards.

We show that every other word can reach the decreasing word with the same number of ones. Choose the lexicographically largest word reachable from it, with $1>0$. It contains neither $001$ nor $011$, since reversing either block is legal and increases the word. Consequently it has the form
$$1^a(01)^b0^c.$$
If it is neither decreasing nor fully alternating, it contains $1101$ or $0100$: this follows by looking at the junction between a repeated initial or final symbol and the alternating portion. But the legal two-move transformations
$$1101\longrightarrow0111\longrightarrow1110,
\qquad0100\longrightarrow0001\longrightarrow1000$$
increase lexicographic order, a contradiction. Thus the maximum reachable word is decreasing, unless the starting word was one of the isolated alternating words.

There are $2023$ possible numbers of ones, giving $2023$ ordinary components, and the two additional isolated words. Taking one representative from each component gives the result.

idn_2022_national_q8.reason: Convexity of the Euclidean norm reduces a three-variable sharp inequality to cube vertices; two nontrivial vertex types determine the constant.
idn_2022_national_q8.note: National. Reviewed all 8 national tasks in each of 2021 and 2022 and all 12 provincial tasks (8 short answer, 4 proof) in the 2024 booklet. Primary author solution archive; not represented as an official organizing-body publication.
idn_2022_national_q8.solutionOverride:
The answer is $K=\sqrt{2/3}$. For fixed $K$, the left side minus the right side is a concave function on the unit cube: its affine part is both convex and concave, and the negative of the Euclidean norm is concave by the triangle inequality. Every point of the cube is a convex combination of its vertices. Therefore it suffices to verify the inequality at vertices.

At a vertex with $j$ coordinates equal to one, it becomes
$$K+j/3\ge(K+1)\sqrt{j/3}.$$
The cases $j=0,3$ are automatic. For $j=1$, rearranging gives $K\ge1/\sqrt3$; for $j=2$, it gives $K\ge\sqrt{2/3}$. Thus the stated value is both sufficient and necessary, with necessity witnessed by $(1,1,0)$.

idn_2024_province_short_q6.note: Provincial short answer. Reviewed all 8 national tasks in each of 2021 and 2022 and all 12 provincial tasks (8 short answer, 4 proof) in the 2024 booklet. Primary author solution archive; not represented as an official organizing-body publication.
idn_2024_province_short_q6.solutionOverride:
Write the side length as $a\sqrt3$, and set $\beta=\angle XBC$. Symmetry across $AC$ gives $\angle XDC=\beta$. The relevant angles are
$$\angle AXB=45^\circ+\beta,\quad\angle DXC=135^\circ-\beta,\quad\angle AXD=45^\circ+\beta.$$
Adding the two half angles and $\angle AXD$ shows $\angle UXV=135^\circ+\beta$. Thus $\beta=15^\circ$, $\angle AXU=30^\circ$, and $\angle DXU=90^\circ$.

Consequently $A,U,X,D$ are cyclic. Their angles give $AU=a$, $DU=2a$, and $DX=XU=a\sqrt2$. Ptolemy's theorem gives
$$AX=\frac{a(\sqrt6+\sqrt2)}2,\qquad XC=\frac{a(\sqrt6-\sqrt2)}2.$$
The bisector theorem in $DXC$ yields $DV/VC=DX/XC=\sqrt3+1$, hence $DV=(3-\sqrt3)a$. The horizontal separation of $U,V$ is therefore $(2-\sqrt3)a$, and their vertical separation is $a\sqrt3$. Thus
$$UV^2=(10-4\sqrt3)a^2=\frac{32+8\sqrt3}{3}.$$
Since $13<8\sqrt3<14$, the required integer is $45$.

idn_2024_province_proof_q4.solutionOverride:
Work modulo the prime $p=2027$; the given interval supplies each residue once. Cubing permutes the residues because $\gcd(3,p-1)=1$. For $b=0$, only $a=0$ works, giving one pair.

For $b\ne0$, put $t=a^3/b$. The equation becomes
$$t^2+b^3+1=0.$$
For every residue $t$, the number $-t^2-1$ is nonzero: otherwise $t^2=-1$, impossible since $p\equiv3\pmod4$ (raise to the power $(p-1)/2$ and use Fermat's theorem). As cubing is bijective, there is a unique nonzero $b$ with $b^3=-t^2-1$, and then a unique $a$ with $a^3=bt$. Thus the nonzero-$b$ case gives exactly $2027$ pairs, for a total of $2028$.

bgd_2024_national_junior_q5.note: Official national paper obtained from the public Drive archive linked by https://matholympiad.org.bd/resources/bdmo-questions. Independent mathematical review; gaps remain explicitly pending.
bgd_2024_national_junior_q5.solutionOverride:
Put $m=\lfloor x\rfloor$. If $m\ge0$, then $m\le x<m+1$, so $m^2\le mx<m(m+1)$. The square bounds force $m\le44$, but then $mx<44\cdot45=1980$, impossible.

If $m<0$, write $m=-k$ with $k>0$. Then $-k\le x<-k+1$, so $k(k-1)<-kx\le k^2$. To have $2024\le-kx<2025$, we need $k=45$: $k\le44$ makes the upper bound too small, while $k\ge46$ makes the lower bound too large. For $k=45$, solving gives
$$-45<x\le-\frac{2024}{45}.$$
Every number in this interval has integer part $-45$ and satisfies the original equation.

bgd_2024_national_junior_q7.reason: A parity count of differently colored pairs, grouped by their unique midpoint, proves that the number of rainbow isosceles triangles is odd.
bgd_2024_national_junior_q7.note: Official national paper obtained from the public Drive archive linked by https://matholympiad.org.bd/resources/bdmo-questions. Independent mathematical review; gaps remain explicitly pending.
bgd_2024_national_junior_q7.solutionOverride:
Label the vertices modulo $17$. Every unordered pair $\{u,v\}$ has a unique midpoint vertex $w$ satisfying $2w=u+v$. Thus every pair determines an isosceles triangle with apex $w$.

The number of pairs with different colors is $RB+BY+YR$, where $R,B,Y$ are the three odd color counts. This number is odd. Such a pair either has a midpoint of the third color, giving the desired triangle, or has a midpoint matching one endpoint.

For each fixed apex $w$, reflection about its radius pairs up the other $16$ vertices. The number of vertices whose color differs from that of $w$ is $17$ minus an odd number, hence even. Therefore an even number of reflection pairs have exactly one endpoint of the apex's color: pairs with two differently colored-from-apex endpoints contribute two to that count, and pairs with one contribute one. Summing over apices, the number of pairs of the second type is even. An odd number remain of the first type, so at least one rainbow isosceles triangle exists.

bgd_2024_national_junior_q8.reason: Normalize the conjugate powers by 2^n; their sum has an integer recurrence that preserves odd parity.
bgd_2024_national_junior_q8.note: Official national paper obtained from the public Drive archive linked by https://matholympiad.org.bd/resources/bdmo-questions. Independent mathematical review; gaps remain explicitly pending.
bgd_2024_national_junior_q8.solutionOverride:
Put $\alpha=(5+\sqrt{17})/2$, $\beta=(5-\sqrt{17})/2$ and $s_n=\alpha^n+\beta^n$. Since $\alpha+\beta=5$ and $\alpha\beta=2$,
$$s_0=2,\quad s_1=5,\quad s_n=5s_{n-1}-2s_{n-2}.$$
Thus all $s_n$ are integers, and every $s_n$ with $n\ge1$ is odd. The expression in the question equals $2^n(5^n-s_n)$. Its parenthesis is an even integer, proving the claim.

bgd_2024_national_secondary_q2.solutionOverride:
Let $EA=a$, $EB=b$, $EC=c$, $ED=d$. Power of $E$ gives $ac=bd$. Orient $AC$ from $E$ toward $C$ and $BD$ from $E$ toward $D$. The signed coordinates of $F,G$ on their lines are $b-a$ and $d-c$, respectively. Therefore
$$\overline{EF}\,\overline{EC}=c(b-a)=bc-ac=bc-bd=(-b)(d-c)=\overline{EB}\,\overline{EG}.$$
By the converse of the intersecting-secants theorem, $B,G,F,C$ lie on one circle. As usual, the construction is understood to have distinct points so that this circle is defined.

bgd_2024_national_secondary_q6.reason: The integer difference of neighboring entries bounds each summand by a reciprocal variation; total variation across the extreme reciprocals is sharp in sorted order.
bgd_2024_national_secondary_q6.note: Official national paper obtained from the public Drive archive linked by https://matholympiad.org.bd/resources/bdmo-questions. Independent mathematical review; gaps remain explicitly pending. Also Higher Secondary Problem 3; identical appearance merged.
bgd_2024_national_secondary_q6.solutionOverride:
For distinct positive integers $a,b$, put $d=|a-b|\ge1$. Since $d^2+1\ge2d$,
$$(a+b)(1/a+1/b)+1/(ab)=4+\frac{d^2+1}{ab}
\ge4+2\left|\frac1a-\frac1b\right|.$$
The sum of the absolute successive differences of a sequence is at least the difference between its largest and smallest entries. Applied to the reciprocals, this gives a lower bound
$$4\cdot2023+2\left(1-\frac1{2024}\right)=8094-\frac1{1012}.$$
The increasing permutation attains equality: every adjacent difference is one and the reciprocals are monotone. This is the minimum.

bgd_2024_national_secondary_q7.reason: A coordinate system at the square vertex makes one constructed line vertical; the two remaining intersection formulas cancel in a dot product.
bgd_2024_national_secondary_q7.note: Official national paper obtained from the public Drive archive linked by https://matholympiad.org.bd/resources/bdmo-questions. Independent mathematical review; gaps remain explicitly pending. Also Higher Secondary Problem 2; identical appearance merged.
bgd_2024_national_secondary_q7.solutionOverride:
Take $B=(0,0)$, $C=(1,0)$, $D=(1,1)$, $A=(0,1)$ and write $E=(0,t)$, $F=(t,0)$, where $0<t<1$. Line $CE$ has equation $tx+y=t$, and its perpendicular through $B$ has equation $y=x/t$. Hence
$$G=\left(\frac{t^2}{1+t^2},\frac{t}{1+t^2}\right),\qquad H=(t,1).$$
Thus $FH$ is vertical, giving $P=(t,t-t^2)$. Intersecting line $GF$ with $x=1$ gives
$$Q=\left(1,\frac{t-1}{t^2-t+1}\right).$$
Now
$$\overrightarrow{DP}\cdot\overrightarrow{BQ}
=(t-1)-(t^2-t+1)\frac{t-1}{t^2-t+1}=0,$$
which proves the perpendicularity.

bgd_2024_national_secondary_q9.reason: Necessity is exposed by n=1 and a prime shared with the step; sufficiency counts multiples of every prime power in an arithmetic progression.
bgd_2024_national_secondary_q9.note: Official national paper obtained from the public Drive archive linked by https://matholympiad.org.bd/resources/bdmo-questions. Independent mathematical review; gaps remain explicitly pending.
bgd_2024_national_secondary_q9.solutionOverride:
Exactly the pairs with $\gcd(m,k!)=1$ work. If a prime $p\le k$ divides $m$, set $n=1$. None of the factors is divisible by $p$, although $k!$ is, so the property fails.

Conversely assume $m$ has no prime divisor at most $k$. Fix a prime $p\le k$. For every $e\ge1$, multiplication by $m$ is invertible modulo $p^e$. Thus among any $p^e$ consecutive indices $i$, exactly one makes $n+im$ divisible by $p^e$. Among $1\le i\le k$ there are at least $\lfloor k/p^e\rfloor$ such indices. Summing over $e$ shows that the product's $p$-adic valuation is at least
$$\sum_{e\ge1}\left\lfloor\frac{k}{p^e}\right\rfloor=v_p(k!).$$
This holds for every prime factor of $k!$, proving divisibility.

bgd_2024_national_higher_secondary_q1.reason: Cubic residues modulo 13 combine with the order of 3 to force p=13; the small prime-exponent exception is checked separately.
bgd_2024_national_higher_secondary_q1.note: Official national paper obtained from the public Drive archive linked by https://matholympiad.org.bd/resources/bdmo-questions. Independent mathematical review; gaps remain explicitly pending.
bgd_2024_national_higher_secondary_q1.solutionOverride:
For $q=3$, the equation gives $p^3=37$, impossible. For any other prime $q$, its residue modulo $3$ is $1$ or $2$. Since $3^3\equiv1\pmod{13}$, we have $3^q\equiv3$ or $9\pmod{13}$, respectively. Thus $p^3\equiv0$ or $6\pmod{13}$.

The cubic residues modulo $13$ are $0,1,5,8,12$, so $6$ is impossible. Hence $13\mid p$, and primality gives $p=13$. Substitution yields $3^q=13^3-10=2187=3^7$. Therefore the sole pair is $(p,q)=(13,7)$.

bgd_2024_national_higher_secondary_q5.reason: The incenter projection and a parallel tangent have explicit coordinates; a side-length identity makes both the scalar and cross products of the angle pairs agree.
bgd_2024_national_higher_secondary_q5.note: Official national paper obtained from the public Drive archive linked by https://matholympiad.org.bd/resources/bdmo-questions. Independent mathematical review; gaps remain explicitly pending.
bgd_2024_national_higher_secondary_q5.solutionOverride:
Choose $B=(0,0)$, $C=(a,0)$, $A=(v,h)$, with $h>0$. Let $b=CA$, $c=AB$, $s=(a+b+c)/2$, and let $r$ be the inradius. The incircle's contact point on $BC$ has coordinate $u=s-b$, so $I=(u,r)$, $P=(u,h)$ and $2r=ah/s$. The upper tangent is $y=2r$, giving
$$Q=(2rv/h,2r),\qquad R=(a+2r(v-a)/h,2r).$$
The cosine rule gives $2av=a^2+c^2-b^2$. Using this and $2u=a+c-b$, direct simplification gives
$$h(a-2u)+2r(v-a+u)=0.\tag{1}$$
Now the cross products of the ordered vector pairs $(PB,PQ)$ and $(PC,PR)$ both equal $2r(v-u)$. Their dot products differ by
$$a(a-2u)+\frac{2ra}{h}(v-a+u),$$
which is zero by (1). Equal cross and dot products imply equal directed angles, and hence the stated ordinary angles. This also covers the zero-cross-product case by continuity whenever the indicated angles are defined.

bgd_2024_national_higher_secondary_q7.reason: A large denominator fixes f(1), then the equation makes f an involution; a diagonal substitution bounds f(n) by n and forces equality.
bgd_2024_national_higher_secondary_q7.note: Official national paper obtained from the public Drive archive linked by https://matholympiad.org.bd/resources/bdmo-questions. Independent mathematical review; gaps remain explicitly pending.
bgd_2024_national_higher_secondary_q7.solutionOverride:
Set $m=1$ and choose $n\ge f(1)$. Both ceilings then equal $1$, so $f(1)=1$. Taking $n=1$ gives $f(f(m))=m$, in particular $f$ is injective.

Suppose $f(n)>n$ for some $n$. Setting $m=n$ makes the right side $1$, while the argument on the left is $\lceil f(n)/n\rceil\ge2$. This contradicts injectivity because $f(1)=1$. Hence $f(n)\le n$ for every $n$. Apply this inequality to $f(n)$ to obtain $n=f(f(n))\le f(n)$. Therefore $f(n)=n$ for all $n$, which satisfies the equation.

isr_2023_gillis_q4.solutionOverride:
Let $H$ be the orthocenter. Since each reflection axis passes through $H$,
$$HU=HV=HW=HO.$$
Thus $O,U,V,W$ lie on a circle centered at $H$. Also $OU\parallel BC$, $OV\parallel CA$, and $OW\parallel AB$, because each segment from a point to its reflection is perpendicular to the reflection axis.

Let the first two proposed lines meet at $X$. Using directed angles modulo $180^\circ$ and the cyclicity just obtained,
$$\angle AXB=\angle VWU=\angle VOU=\angle ACB.$$
Hence $A,B,C,X$ are concyclic. Similarly the intersection of the first and third proposed lines lies on the same circumcircle. The line through $A$ has only one second intersection with that circle, so the intersections coincide. Limiting tangent configurations follow by the same directed-angle argument.

isr_2023_gillis_q5.reason: Odd-index divisibility gives one direction; in the other, a simultaneous Fermat exponent avoids every prime below a proposed bound.
isr_2023_gillis_q5.note: All seven tasks in the official paper dated 6 December 2023 were individually reviewed with the official solution booklet. Hebrew year 5784.
isr_2023_gillis_q5.solutionOverride:
Exactly the odd values of $a_1$ work. Parity alternates at every step. Moreover
$$a_{2j+1}=(a_{2j-1}^{,2j-1}-1)^{2j}-1\equiv0\pmod{a_{2j-1}}.$$
Thus every odd-indexed term is divisible by $a_1$. If $a_1$ is odd, all even-indexed terms are even, so the least prime factors are bounded by $\max(2,p(a_1))$.

Conversely suppose $a_1$ is even and the least prime factors are bounded. List all primes below a proposed bound, enlarging the bound if necessary so that both $2$ and $3$ are present. Let $L$ be the product of $p-1$ over these primes, and set $n=L+1$, which is odd. For each such prime $p$, either $p\mid a_L$, or Fermat's theorem gives $a_L^L\equiv1\pmod p$. Hence
$$a_n=a_L^L-1\equiv-1\ \text{or}\ 0\pmod p.$$
Since $n$ is odd, $a_{n+1}=a_n^n-1$ is congruent to $-2$ or $-1$ modulo each odd listed prime, so none divides it. Because $a_1$ is even and $n+1$ is even, parity alternation makes $a_{n+1}$ odd; $2$ does not divide it either. This contradicts the proposed bound.
